question: Q40
question_text: Earlier figures: Cleverdon is the only pre-1970 witness checked. Are there other earlier figures (e.g. interwar women writers of history) the user wants?

what_the_review_says: Coulter: the editors ask about 'the legitimacy of amateur/professional dichotomy as applied to the term historian' (p. 4) and 'just how closely allied historical professionalization was to the masculinization of history' (p. 5).
Coulter: Crowley shows how Isabel Skelton 'sought to write women back into Canadian history'.
Coulter: Prentice raises questions about why women found it easier to hold posts in western Canadian history departments, 'Margaret Ormsby and Hilda Neatby being but two outstanding examples'.

Coulter: the editors acknowledge the lives explored come primarily from 'the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society' and are not necessarily 'typical of the women who have taken up the work of history' (p. 9).
guide.who_the_book_treats: Chapter subjects: Machar, Curzon, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Wood-Legh; collectively the Ontario Women's Institutes and women religious; in Prentice's chapter, women in the professoriate including Ormsby and Neatby (per the review; chapter not read). Agnes Laut, Maude Abbott, Marie Gérin-Lajoie and Catherine Cleverdon are NOT chapter subjects; whether the introduction mentions them is not_verified.

recommendation.framing: Call these 'earlier women writers of history', not founders or practitioners of women's history. Most wrote national, local, regional, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (per Coulter's review of Crowley) and Daveluy (per Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women into the story. Present them through the 1997 recovery: Boutilier and Prentice asked how professionalisation masculinised history and questioned the amateur/professional divide. Note the editors' own caveat that their subjects are mainly white and Anglo-Celtic. Keep Cleverdon (1950) as the one earlier study of women's political history. Neatby and Ormsby are examples of women in the profession, not of the field.
recommendation.draft_sentence_suggestion: Women wrote Canadian history long before the field existed: as popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Clark Wright), as independent scholars such as Isabel Skelton, who 'sought to write women back into Canadian history' (Coulter's reading of Crowley), and as a few university historians (Neatby, Ormsby). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy foregrounded women in the history of New France. Boutilier and Prentice's Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalisation had masculinised history.

caveats: Chapters of Creating Historical Memory were not read; subjects come from titles, the publisher page and one review.
Daveluy and the francophone volume are post-1997 scholarship (2018, 2023); in an atlas covering through 2000 they belong in extension_coverage or as evidence, not as period milestones.
Citation counts are low for every figure except Neatby and Cleverdon; earlier writers are often cited as primary sources.
Laval is thin in the corpus (9 PhDs), so francophone counts for Daveluy are undercounts.
